blocks.title: Cis-trans isomers
blocks.text: The stereoisomers having different spatial arrangement of atoms due to restricted rotation about a double bond in open chain compounds are called cis-trans isomers.
First of all we consider free rotation about C-C single bond in butane.

blocks.alt: Two drawings of butane, I and II, joined by an arrow with a rotation sign. In I, carbon 2 carries CH3 (carbon 1) at the upper left and two H; carbon 3 carries two H and CH3 (carbon 4) at the lower right. In II, rotation about the C2-C3 bond has moved carbon 1 to the lower left (H3C), with H at the upper left and left; carbon 3 is unchanged.
blocks.caption: Two forms (I and II) of butane interconverted by rotation about the C2-C3 single bond (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: In butane, forms I or II are called conformational isomers because they are interconvertable into each other due to free rotation of the C-C single bond. They cannot be separated at room temperature.
When the C-C single bond between C-2 and C-3 atoms rotates, the methyl groups also rotate and structure I changes in II and II back into I due to this free rotation.

Now, consider but-2-ene CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃ in which both carbon atoms 2 and 3 are sp² hybridized. The C-C double bond consists of a σ bond formed by the linear overlap of sp² hybrid orbitals and a π bond formed by the parallel overlap of ρ orbitals. The presence of π bond locks the molecule in one position. The two carbon atoms C-2 and C-3 of the double bond and all the groups attached to them lie in the same plane and their position in space is fixed. For free rotation around the C-C double bond, π bond should be broken first. It requires energy equal to 263 kJ/mol, which is not possible at room temperature. The rotation about C-C double bond is therefore restricted. This restriction of rotation about the C-C double bond is responsible for the cis-trans isomerism (Figure 19.6).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The π bond is formed by the sideways (parallel) overlap of p orbitals; the printed “ρ” (the Greek letter rho) should be the letter p.

blocks.alt: Three drawings of but-2-ene, p orbitals as blue lobes. Cis: two C joined, each with lobes up and down overlapping above and below (the pi bond, with an electron pair); H on hashed bonds at the top, H3C and CH3 on wedges below. Middle: one carbon turned through 90 degrees so its p orbital is perpendicular to the other, each lobe with one electron: no overlap with the ends perpendicular. Trans: like cis but CH3 top right and H bottom right. Crossed double arrows between them.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.6: The two isomers of but-2-ene cannot interconvert by rotation about the C-C double bond without breaking the pi bond (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.6).

blocks.text: Now the above sturctures can be considered as cis-trans isomers and named as follows.

blocks.alt: Two structural formulae: cis-but-2-ene, C=C with H3C and CH3 both at the top and H and H at the bottom; trans-but-2-ene, C=C with H and CH3 at the top and H3C and H at the bottom.
blocks.caption: Cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure).

blocks.text: The cis isomer is one in which two similar groups are on the same side of the double bond. The trans isomer is that in which two similar groups are on the opposite side of the double bond. blocks.title: Keep in Mind
blocks.text: The cis-trans isomers have different physical and chemical properties. The trans isomers are more stable than the corresponding cis isomers and hence differ in chemical reactivity. Similarly, both types of isomers have different physical properties like melting point, boiling point, dipole moment, density, heat of vapourisation etc.
Each of the above two compounds does not show cis-trans isomerism.

blocks.title: Cis-trans isomerism
blocks.text: “Thus for an open chain compound the necessary and sufficient condition to show cis-trans isomerism is that, it should have double bond in its molecule and that two different groups must be attacked to each of the doubly bonded carbon atoms.”

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The two different groups must be attached (bonded) to each doubly bonded carbon atom; “attacked” is a misprint.
